cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: It’s really good to see you, Tom. Since I had to give up work, I feel I’m losing touch with my friends and colleagues.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: We really miss you in the office. We were all so sorry you had to leave. But you must be relieved to have more time to look after your mother. How is she?

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Well she is very cheerful, but she needs a lot of help.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Have you tried to get any support from the local council?

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: No, I didn’t know I could.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Yes, they offer different kinds of practical support.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: They realise that carers sometimes need time for all the other responsibilities they have, apart from the person they’re caring for, and also that they sometimes need a break.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Absolutely. OK, so tell me more. How do I go about getting this support?

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Well, you’d have to have an assessment of your mother’s needs.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: That means someone would come round and talk to you about the situation and what you need.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: So, for a start, they’d want to know the amount of time you spend looking after your mother every day.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: OK.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Then they’ll probably ask you what sorts of tasks you do for your mother during the day. Things like if she needs help with getting dressed, for example.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Right. I help her with that. And also I help her get into the shower in the morning.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Yes, that sort of thing.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Yes, that’s becoming a bit of a problem. She used to be very good at it, but not anymore.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions five to ten. you Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: And be ready to tell them about anything you find particularly difficult about caring for your mother.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: So, recently I’ve noticed she’s started to have quite bad problems with her memory.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: If I wasn’t there, I think she’d forget to eat, for example.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: And often she doesn’t seem quite sure what day it is.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Yes, tell them about that. And are there any physical difficulties you have caring for her? Lifting her, for example?

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Yes, she’s quite heavy and I’m afraid of hurting my back. I’d be in real trouble if that happened.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: They can give you advice about that and also about how to avoid the possibility of your mum having a fall.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Great. So once they’ve done this assessment, if I’m eligible, what happens next?

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Well, they might support you financially. So they might help you with transport costs, like if you have to get a taxi to take your mother for an appointment, for example.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: I usually drive her myself, actually. So, could I claim the petrol?

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: You could. And you can claim for the insurance too.

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Oh, right.

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: And if you need help with the housework, they can arrange for someone to come along once or twice a week. And one other thing. I hope you don’t mind me saying this, but it important you

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: look after yourself And it seems to me you under quite a bit of stress

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: I am yes

cues.speaker: MAN
cues.text: Well tell the council because they may be able to give you some advice on how to minimise it

cues.speaker: WOMAN
cues.text: Really? Though, actually, I feel so much better having talked to you. I’ll get in touch with the council straight away. Now, shall we go for coffee or something?
